words.meaning: making someone very weak and unable to function normally

words.meaning: the physical or mental strength to keep going for a long time

words.meaning: involving little movement or physical activity; sitting a lot
words.example: A sedentary lifestyle increases the risk of heart disease.

words.meaning: natural, pure, and good for your health
words.example: She prefers wholesome, unprocessed foods over packaged snacks.

words.meaning: a mild illness or health problem
words.example: The clinic treats every minor ailment, from colds to sprains.

words.meaning: a treatment or solution that cures a health problem
words.example: Rest and hydration remain the simplest remedy for a common cold.

words.meaning: the body's natural protection against disease
words.example: Vaccination strengthens your immunity against the virus.

words.meaning: the period of recovering from an illness or operation
words.example: During his convalescence, he took long walks by the sea.

grammar.title: 3A: Choosing between comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation:
Use **comparative adjectives + than** to compare two people, places, or things. Short adjectives take **-er**; longer ones take **more**.

Spelling matters: **big → bigger**, **easy → easier**, **hot → hotter**. One-syllable adjectives ending in **-ed** take **more**: **more tired**, **more stressed**.

Three adjectives are irregular: **good → better**, **bad → worse**, **far → further** (use **farther** only for physical distance).

To show equality, use **(not) as + adjective + as**: her recovery was as swift as his. **The same as** marks identical things: his symptoms were the same as mine.

Comparative adverbs compare actions, not things: she walks **faster than** me; he breathes **more deeply than** before. Two are irregular: **well → better**, **badly → worse**.

Use **the + superlative** to single out one member of a group: the **tallest** player, the **most expensive** clinic. **The least** marks the bottom of the scale.

After a superlative, say **in** — never **of** — with places: the best hospital **in** the city. Superlatives love the **present perfect + ever**: the hardest convalescence I have **ever** faced.

At C2, the double comparative shows elegant cause and effect: **the more sedentary the lifestyle, the weaker the immunity**. Both halves use **the + comparative**.

Choose comparatives for two items and superlatives for three or more. Comparing your stamina today with yesterday's needs a comparative; ranking every remedy you tried needs a superlative.

Nuance check: **further** also means additional, as in further treatment, while **farther** is strictly distance. And **elder/eldest** describe family seniority, not just age.

Sophisticated speakers intensify comparisons: a **far more debilitating** ailment, a **much more wholesome** diet, **by far the most invigorating** therapy. **Far**, **much**, and **by far** sharpen the contrast.

For the ultimate C2 touch, compare abstract qualities: no remedy promises **greater longevity** than consistent, wholesome habits. Abstract nouns take these structures beautifully.
examples: The mountain air was *more invigorating* than any energy drink. (comparative + than)
Chronic fatigue is *more debilitating* than most people imagine.
Her *stamina* is *greater than* mine after only a month of training.
A desk job is *more sedentary than* nursing, which keeps you on your feet.
This soup is *as wholesome as* anything my grandmother made. ((not) as + adjective + as)
It was the *mildest ailment* I have *ever* had, barely worth a doctor's visit. (superlative + present perfect + ever)
Of every *remedy* we tried, rest proved *the most effective*.
Okinawans enjoy *greater longevity than* almost any other population.
His *immunity* recovered *faster than* the doctors had predicted. (comparative adverb)
It was *the longest convalescence* of her life, and also the most peaceful.
*The more invigorating* the morning routine, *the stronger* the immunity all winter. (double comparative)
She felt *far better* after switching to a *more wholesome* diet. (irregular + intensifier)

practice.q: Complete: Regular exercise is ___ (beneficial) than any expensive supplement.
Which is correct: 'the best hospital of the city' or 'the best hospital in the city'? Why?
practice.a: 'the best hospital in the city' — use in, not of, after superlatives with places.

practice.q: Rewrite with a double comparative: A sedentary routine weakens immunity a lot.
practice.a: The more sedentary the routine, the weaker the immunity.
